items.title: Meta made scam ads harder to find instead of removing them
items.raw_content: In its latest piece on Meta’s scam ads, Reuters found that the social media giant didn’t just remove fraudulent ads from its platforms — it also worked to make them harder for governments and journalists to find. Fearing that Japanese regulators would require universal advertiser verification — a measure Meta estimated would cost roughly $2 billion to implement and potentially reduce its revenue by nearly 5% — the company took steps to make scam ads less “discoverable” to “regulators, investigators and journalists,” according to internal documents reviewed by Reuters.
items.title_zh: Meta 没有清除诈骗广告，而是让它们更难被找到
items.summary: Reuters reported, based on internal documents, that Meta went beyond removing fraudulent ads and also worked to make them harder for regulators, investigators and journalists to uncover. The company acted amid concern that Japanese regulators could require universal advertiser verification, which Meta estimated would cost about $2 billion and reduce revenue by nearly 5%.

items.title: iOS allows alternative browser engines in Japan
items.raw_content: In iOS 26.2 and later, browser engines other than WebKit can be used in two types of apps for users in Japan: Dedicated browser apps that provide a full web browser experience, and apps from browser engine stewards that provide in-app browsing experiences using an embedded browser engine. Apple will provide authorized developers access to technologies within the system that enable critical functionality and help them offer high-performance modern browser engines. These technologies include just-in-time compilation, multiprocess support, and more.
items.title_zh: iOS 在日本允许使用替代浏览器引擎
items.summary: Apple's documentation states that starting with iOS 26.2, users in Japan can use non-WebKit browser engines in two categories of app: dedicated browsers, and apps from engine stewards that provide embedded in-app browsing. Developers with authorization will gain access to capabilities such as just-in-time compilation and multiprocess support.

items.title: Can Bundler be as fast as uv?
items.raw_content: At RailsWorld earlier this year, I got nerd sniped by someone. They asked âwhy canât Bundler be as fast as uv?â Immediately my inner voice said âYA, WHY CANâT IT BE AS FAST AS UV????â My inner voice likes to shout at me, especially when someone asks a question so obvious I should have thought of it myself. Since then Iâve been thinking about and investigating this problem, going so far as to give a presentation at XO Ruby Portland about Bundler performance. I firmly believe the answer is âBundler can be as fast as uvâ (where âas fastâ has a margin of error lol).
items.title_zh: Bundler 能像 uv 一样快吗？
items.summary: The author recounts being challenged at RailsWorld to explain why Bundler cannot match uv's speed, and says he has since investigated the question and given a talk on Bundler performance at XO Ruby Portland. items.title: Show HN: OpenWorkers – Self-hosted Cloudflare workers in Rust
items.raw_content: I've been working on this for some time now, starting with vm2, then deno-core for 2 years, and recently rewrote it on rusty_v8 with Claude's help. OpenWorkers lets you run untrusted JS in V8 isolates on your own infrastructure. Same DX as Cloudflare Workers, no vendor lock-in. What works today: fetch, KV, Postgres bindings, S3/R2, cron scheduling, crypto.subtle. Self-hosting is a single docker-compose file + Postgres. Would love feedback on the architecture and what feature you'd want next.
items.title_zh: Show HN：OpenWorkers——用 Rust 自托管的 Cloudflare Workers
items.summary: The developer describes OpenWorkers as a way to run untrusted JavaScript in V8 isolates on your own infrastructure, with a Cloudflare Workers-like developer experience and no vendor lock-in. Current capabilities include fetch, KV, Postgres bindings, S3/R2 and cron scheduling, with self-hosting via a single docker-compose file plus Postgres.

items.title: Dell's version of the DGX Spark fixes pain points
items.raw_content: Dell sent me two of their GB10 mini workstations to test: In this blog post, I'll cover the base system, just one of the two nodes. Cluster testing is ongoing, and I'll cover things like AI model training and networking more in depth next year, likely with comparisons to the Framework Desktop cluster and Mac Studio cluster I've also been testing. But many of the same caveats of the DGX Spark (namely, price to performance is not great if you just want to run LLMs on a small desktop) apply to Dell's GB10 box as well.
items.title_zh: 戴尔版 DGX Spark 解决了此前的痛点
items.summary: Jeff Geerling tested two of Dell's GB10 mini workstations and reviews the base system, with cluster testing, AI model training and networking coverage to follow. He notes that the same caveat as the DGX Spark applies: price-to-performance is not great if the goal is simply running LLMs on a small desktop.

items.title: Show HN: Enroll, a tool to reverse-engineer servers into Ansible config mgmt
items.raw_content: Happy new year folks! This tool was born out of a situation where I had 'inherited' a bunch of servers that were not under any form of config management. Oh, the horror... Enroll 'harvests' system information such as what packages are installed, what services are running, what files have 'differed' from their out-of-the-box defaults, and what other custom snowflake data might exist. The harvest state data can be kept as its own sort of SBOM, but also can be converted in a mere second or two into fully-functional Ansible roles/playbooks/inventory. It can be run remotely over SSH or locally on the machine. Debian and Redhat-like systems are supported. There is also a 'diff' mode to detect drift over time. (Years ago I used Puppet instead of Ansible and miss the agent/server model where it would check in and re-align to the expected state, in case people were being silly and side-stepping t
items.title_zh: Show HN：Enroll——把服务器逆向为 Ansible 配置管理的工具
items.summary: The author built Enroll after inheriting servers that were not under any configuration management; it harvests installed packages, running services, files that differ from defaults and other custom state. That data can be kept as an SBOM or converted into Ansible roles, playbooks and inventory, and it runs over SSH or locally on Debian and Red Hat-like systems, with a diff mode to detect drift.
